title: Fortification
subtitle: The spirit and the timing
objectives: Explain the chemistry of stopping fermentation

steps.title: The spirit
steps.body: Fortifying spirit is grape spirit, usually distilled to between 77 and 96%. Port uses aguardente at about 77%, which carries some flavour of its own. Sherry and most vins doux naturels use neutral spirit at around 95 to 96%, which adds alcohol without flavour. Less spirit is needed when it's stronger.

steps.title: Stopping the yeast
steps.body: Yeast can't work above about 15 to 16% alcohol. Adding spirit mid-fermentation pushes the wine past that point, killing the yeast and keeping the remaining sugar. In Port, about 115 litres of spirit go into 435 litres of fermenting must, making the classic 550-litre pipe. The earlier the spirit goes in, the sweeter the wine.

steps.prompt: Why does adding spirit mid-fermentation keep a wine sweet?
options: The higher alcohol kills the yeast before it finishes
steps.explanation: Yeast stops working above about 15 to 16% alcohol, leaving the unfermented sugar.

steps.title: Timing and style
steps.body: Spirit added early gives sweet, fruity wines: Port, vins doux naturels and sweet Madeira. Added late, after a dry fermentation, it gives dry wines: Fino, Manzanilla, Sercial Madeira. Each family also uses ageing, with or without oxygen, to shape the final style.

steps.prompt: Match each wine to when spirit is added.
steps.explanation: Timing determines sweetness; strength determines whether flor can grow.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Fortifying spirit ranges from 77% for Port to about 96% for Sherry
Spirit above about 16% alcohol stops the yeast
Early fortification keeps sugar; late fortification keeps the wine dry
